summary: For ages 12–13, Ohm's Law (V = IR) is taught as ONE relationship linking voltage (the push), current (the flow) and resistance (the opposition). Current is proportional to voltage only while resistance stays constant. The relationship is derived from the ratio definition R = V/I rather than memorised as a formula triangle. The core learning is seeing how current responds when you change voltage or resistance, and understanding WHY via a particle picture of charges colliding with the lattice: in a longer wire each charge meets more collisions along the way, and a thinner wire has fewer parallel lanes for charge, so both give more resistance. Activities cover an interactive sandbox for cause-and-effect exploration, a retrieval set for calculation fluency, reference supports, and a Socratic debrief. Note the UK curriculum placement: the V=IR ratio and calculation sit at KS3, while the named 'Ohm's Law' and graphical I–V treatment are KS4 extensions kept qualitative here.
misconceptions: Treating V = IR as a meaningless triangle to shuffle — substituting without knowing which quantity is the push, the flow, or the opposition.
Thinking resistance 'uses up' current — resistance REDUCES the current (everywhere in a series loop) but does not consume charge; the current is still the same all the way round, just smaller.
Believing a thicker wire has MORE resistance — it has LESS (more lanes for charge); thickness and length pull opposite ways.
Assuming current and voltage are always directly proportional — only when resistance is constant; a heating filament's resistance rises, so its V–I line bends (the KS4 caveat).
Confusing which quantity changes when — e.g. expecting changing the resistor to change the battery's voltage; the cell sets V, the circuit's R then sets I.
Mis-rearranging the equation — e.g. writing I = VR instead of I = V/R — from manipulating symbols without the proportional sense (more opposition must mean less current).
Equating 'Ohm's Law' with all components — it describes the constant-resistance (ohmic) case; not every component obeys a single straight-line relationship.

activities.title: Ohm's Law sandbox: change the push, change the opposition
steps: Set a battery to 3 V across a resistor and read the current on a live ammeter.
Keeping the same resistor (constant resistance), drag the voltage to 6 V and watch the current double in real time — put twice the push in, get twice the flow.
Holding the voltage fixed, make the wire thicker and watch the current climb; lengthen it and watch the current fall.
Try a material swap to see that different materials give different resistance for the same size of wire.

Toggle a particle view that shows charges colliding with the lattice: observe that in a longer wire each charge meets more collisions along the way, and that a thinner wire has fewer parallel lanes for charge, so fewer charges get through per second.
Use a 'predict the ammeter, then reveal' mode: commit a value for the current before the meter is uncovered on each change.
Optionally switch on a filament mode where the resistance climbs as the wire heats, so the current no longer simply doubles when the voltage doubles — a qualitative preview of the KS4 non-ohmic case.
Read V = IR updating beside every move and say aloud which quantity is the push, which is the flow, and which is the opposition.
activities.insight: V = IR is a description of cause and effect the learner controls: for a fixed resistance, doubling the voltage doubles the current; for a fixed voltage, doubling the resistance halves the current. The factor effects (longer = more resistance, thicker = less resistance, material matters) become causal through the collision picture, not memorised. The optional filament mode shows that this neat proportionality holds only while resistance stays constant.

activities.title: Calculate and reason: V, I, R fluency set
steps: Solve fill-in/numeric V=IR problems with friendly numbers: find I given V and R; find R given V and I; find V given I and R.
Answer proportional-reasoning questions such as 'voltage doubles, resistance stays the same — what happens to the current?' (it doubles).

Sort changes — longer wire / shorter wire / thicker wire / thinner wire — into 'more resistance' vs 'less resistance', and note that changing to a different material can give either more or less resistance depending on which material is used.
Spot the wrong rearrangement: identify that I = VR is incorrect and that I = V/R is right, explaining that more opposition must mean less current.
Write the correct unit beside each answer (volts, amperes, ohms) and say which unit belongs to which quantity.
activities.insight: Learners can rearrange the single relationship for any unknown, attach correct units, and use proportional reasoning rather than rote substitution. Catching I = VR as wrong comes from the proportional sense, not from symbol-manipulation alone.

activities.title: Quick reference: the relationship and the particle picture
steps: Tap each symbol in R = V/I / V = IR / I = V/R to reveal its quantity, unit and plain-words meaning ('current is push divided by opposition').
Tap a longer or thinner wire in a labelled diagram to reveal 'more resistance', and a thicker wire to reveal 'less resistance'.
Use the reference alongside the sandbox or the calculation set as a memory aid, not as the main teacher.
activities.insight: The three forms R = V/I, V = IR and I = V/R are rearrangements of ONE relationship, each readable in words; the factor effects can be recalled with a labelled picture.

activities.title: Engineer debrief: what happens to the current if...?
steps: Respond to an engineer persona posing 'what happens to I if...' scenarios (e.g. 'you halved the resistance — what should the current do, and why?').
Explain the reason behind each prediction, not just the direction of change.
Correct, with guidance, the triangle-shuffle habit and the 'thicker wire = more resistance' error when they arise.
Articulate that resistance opposes and reduces current everywhere in a series loop but does not consume the charge.
activities.insight: Learners can reason aloud about proportional changes and defend why, cementing 'resistance opposes, not consumes' and the inverse factor links.

checkQuestion: Work these three on paper while I watch — show your steps and your units. (a) A 6 V battery drives 2 A through a lamp; find its resistance. (b) A 12 Ω resistor has 3 V across it; find the current through it. (c) A wire carries 0.5 A when 4 V is applied. You swap it for a wire of the same metal and thickness but twice as long — will the current go up or down, and roughly to what? Talk me through nothing in advance; just work, and I'll ask afterwards.
checkAnswer: (a) R = V/I = 6/2 = 3 Ω. (b) I = V/R = 3/12 = 0.25 A. (c) Doubling the length doubles the resistance, so for the same 4 V the current halves — to about 0.25 A (it goes down).
